documents.abstract: Background: The use of digital health technologies, such as chatbots and virtual assistants based on artificial intelligence, has grown significantly in maternal health. These tools have been applied at different stages of the pregnancy and postpartum cycle, with emphasis on health education, risk monitoring, breastfeeding support, and mental healthcare. Despite their potential, challenges remain regarding clinical effectiveness, equity of access, and ethical safety. The aim of this study was to map the available evidence regarding the applications of artificial intelligence in pregnancy, childbirth, and postpartum care, with particular emphasis on conversational agents, virtual assistants, machine learning models, and clinical decision support systems, as well as their potential benefits, limitations, ethical implications, and implementation challenges. Methods: A scoping review was conducted between August and September 2025 in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Nursing Database, Latin American and Caribbean Literature in Health Sciences, and Google Scholar. Original articles, reviews, experience reports, and theoretical reflections published in Portuguese, English, or Spanish that addressed the use of digital tools based on artificial intelligence in the pregnancy and postpartum cycle were included. The analysis of the studies was organized into five thematic axes: applications in prenatal care; support during childbirth; postpartum monitoring and breastfeeding; perinatal mental health; and ethical, technical, and implementation challenges. Results: The search identified 6230 records, of which 13 studies were included. Findings indicate that chatbots and virtual assistants show good acceptability, promote health education, and contribute to the early detection of physical and emotional risks. However, most of the studies are exploratory, with methodological limitations, lack of clinical trials, and limited validation in socially vulnerable contexts. Conclusions: Chatbots and artificial intelligence tools are promising resources for perinatal care, particularly as a complement to face-to-face attention. Their consolidation requires robust studies, cost-effectiveness assessments, and public policies that ensure equity and digital inclusion.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly positioned at the intersection of business transformation and sustainable development. Its capacity to identify patterns in large datasets, forecast demand and risk, automate routine processes, support product innovation, and improve resource allocation creates opportunities to enhance organizational performance while addressing environmental and social priorities. Yet these outcomes are not automatic: AI can reproduce bias, intensify surveillance, displace or transform work, widen digital inequalities, and consume substantial energy and material resources. This conceptual study synthesizes the supplied literature review on AI-enabled sustainability, digital transformation, innovation, governance, and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). It develops an integrated framework in which AI capabilities influence sustainable business transformation through three complementary mechanisms: operational and resource optimization, innovation capability, and data-driven decision-making. The proposed framework links AI adoption with economic, environmental, and social sustainability through digital infrastructure, workforce skills, organizational readiness, and collaboration. Responsible governance, fairness, accountability, and data protection ensure ethical implementation. AI-driven sustainability requires strategic alignment, organizational learning, and responsible practices to achieve measurable business transformation and sustainable outcomes. As a conceptual paper, it does not claim empirical validation; instead, it offers propositions and a research agenda for future survey, case-study, and structural-equation modelling research.

documents.abstract: Peer review is important in maintaining the quality of scholarly publishing, but the process faces challenges such as shortage of reviewers, delays, inconsistent judgements, and overlooked errors. These challenges have increased the need to consider the appropriate use of artificial intelligence (AI) in peer review. Completely excluding AI or allowing it to function as an autonomous reviewer may not adequately address these problems. A Human–AI Augmented Review model is therefore proposed, in which AI supports clearly defined tasks under human supervision, while reviewers and editors retain responsibility for interpretation, ethical judgement, and editorial decisions. Peer review involves both routine technical checks and complex scholarly evaluation. AI can assist with repetitive and rule-based tasks such as manuscript screening, consistency checking, reviewer identification, and identification of reporting gaps. Human reviewers are still needed to assess methodology, scholarly contribution, and ethical issues. Effective use of AI requires a clear division of responsibilities, verification points within the review process, and governance measures to address bias, hallucinations, confidentiality, and excessive reliance on automation. Careful and limited use of AI can improve efficiency and reduce avoidable errors while maintaining accountability and trust in peer review.

Introduction: Gastrointestinal disorders involve interacting digestive, emotional, sleep, and behavioral factors requiring longitudinal assessment. Objective: To evaluate 12-week feasibility, engagement, and clinical associations of a mobile AI-driven mental health assistant in adults with gastrointestinal disorders. Methods: This prospective comparative study enrolled 186 Venezuelan adults with irritable bowel syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease, functional dyspepsia, or gastroesophageal reflux disease. Participants were assigned to a mobile AI assistant plus standard medical care (n=94) or standard medical care (n=92). The intervention combined conversational support, journaling, and emotional self-reports with required wearable-based monitoring (e.g., smartwatch and smart ring). Both groups underwent assessment of sleep, resting heart rate, nocturnal heart-rate variability, and daily steps. The primary outcome was symptomatic days per week. GAD-7 and PHQ-9 assessed anxiety and depression; adjusted differences included 95% confidence intervals. Results: Participant retention was 91.5% in the intervention group and 85.9% in the standard medical care group, with fewer symptomatic days, reduced anxiety and depression, and 28 additional minutes of sleep nightly. Resting heartrate decreased by 3.6 beats/min and nocturnal RMSSD increased by 5.1 ms relative to comparison; both confidence intervals excluded zero. Daily-step differences were nonsignificant. Daily check-in completion among enrolled participants was 74.8%. Conclusions: The mobile AI intervention was associated with improvements in gastrointestinal symptoms, emotional outcomes, sleep, and autonomic measures.ESCUCHE EL RESUMEN HANCIENDO CLIC EN EL IDIOMA DE SU PREFERENCIA:EspañolEnglishPortugués Japones

Lifestyle counseling is central to cardiovascular prevention, yet recommendations may be difficult to communicate within routine consultations and to translate into feasible daily actions. This perspective proposes a clinician supervised framework in which artificial intelligence helps draft patient readable lifestyle plans from explicitly approved clinical instructions. The framework separates deterministic safety rules and curated clinical content from language generation; a template system without machine learning is recognized as a valid alternative. Personalization is limited to clinician verified information and patient stated preferences, including language, food affordability, and practical access to physical activity. Proposed safeguards include data minimization, version controlled source material, documented review, patient clarification, and escalation when inputs are incomplete or conflicting. Particular attention is given to professional accountability, health literacy, digital exclusion, and the possibility that fluent drafts encourage superficial verification. Lifestyle advice is not assumed to be inherently safe, especially in patients with multimorbidity. This article presents a conceptual proposal rather than an evaluated intervention or systematic review. A staged research agenda compares the approach with high quality nonautomated counseling materials and measures safety, comprehension, clinician workload, equity, and sustained behavior change. Any benefit remains to be established empirically; the intended contribution is a testable model of accountable health communication rather than a claim of improved cardiovascular outcomes.

documents.abstract: Purpose:This study examined undergraduate nursing students’ attitudes toward artificial intelligence and their readiness for medical artificial intelligence, as well as the factors associated with AI readiness.Methods: A descriptive, cross-sectional design was employed. Two hundred and fifty undergraduate nursing students at a nursing faculty in western Türkiye participated during the 2025–2026 academic year. Three instruments were administered: a Participant Information Form, the General Attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence Scale, and the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students.Results: The Positive General Attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence Scale yielded a mean of 3.88 ± 0.66, the Negative General Attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence Scale 3.26 ± 0.87, and the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students 74.29 ± 13.43. Academic year was significantly associated with AI readiness. One-way ANOVA showed significant differences across year groups (F = 3.450; p = 0.012; η² = 0.040), with fourth-year students scoring higher than second-year students. In the multiple linear regression analysis, both second-year (β = −0.156, p = 0.014) and third-year (β = −0.143, p = 0.024) students had significantly lower readiness scores compared with fourth-year students. A moderate positive correlation was observed between positive AI attitudes and readiness scores(r = 0.430; p < 0.01). Positive attitudes toward AI and self-reported computer skills emerged as the strongest independent factors associated with readiness.Conclusion: Nursing students displayed generally favorable attitudes toward AI, yet readiness levels varied across academic years. Attitude and readiness, while correlated, appear to be distinct constructs. These findings highlight the need for intentional, practice-oriented integration of AI competencies into undergraduate nursing curricula.

documents.abstract: As a result of the blistering emergence of the digital ecosystem, the cases of cybercrime have risen at an alarming rate, and it is a significant challenge to all law enforcement agencies and forensic investigators. Traditional investigation techniques are often not adequate to manage the volume, scope, and rate of the existing cyber threats. This chapter, Artificial Intelligence for Cybercrime Investigation and Forensics, talks of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and its use in investigating and preventing cybercrimes in terms of how automation, predictive modeling, and smart data interpretation will enable easier identification and solve cybercrime cases. It discusses various AI paradigms, such as Deep Learning, Natural Language Processing, and Computer Vision, which can help to raise the accuracy and efficiency of forensics. The other area that the chapter covers is the use of AI to identify threats, profile behaviors, authenticate evidence, and even create digital traces, and this provides an overall picture of how AI has been impacting the improvement of cyber justice systems. Furthermore, it describes significant ethical, legal, and technical challenges, including the privacy of data, bias of algorithms, and the application of AI-generated evidence in a court of justice. The chapter gives the readers a glimpse of a future where smart, transparent, and autonomous AI-driven forensic systems can assist in combating the evolving digital threats and still provide the investigations with fairness, accountability, and trust in the online investigations.

Sports talent identification (TID) seeks to detect and select athletes with exceptional potential, but conventional practice relies heavily on coach and scout judgement and is exposed to relative age effects, differences in biological maturation and small-sample intuition. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML), is increasingly proposed as a decision-support tool that can integrate anthropometric, physical, technical, psychosocial and match-tracking data. This paper presents a focused narrative review of verified peer-reviewed studies, prioritising 2019–2026 publications, that apply AI to talent selection, performance prediction, playing-position classification, athlete profiling and scouting. The review examines three connected themes: data sources (field tests, match and tracking data, psychosocial measures, maturation indicators and video), learning methods (penalised regression, tree ensembles, support vector machines, neural networks and unsupervised clustering), and validation and deployment practice. The literature shows that models reach moderate to high internal discrimination, with area under the ROC curve (AUC) values reported from about 0.58 to 0.96 in a recent systematic review, while very high accuracies are usually reported for small or augmented datasets without external validation. Most studies are male-dominated, soccer-dominated and single-club, and few report calibration, fairness audits or prospective testing. The review contributes a comparative analysis of representative studies, a conceptual athlete-to-decision architecture that links multi-source data acquisition, age- and maturation-aware modelling, calibrated and explainable prediction, human-in-the-loop decision support and external validation, and a prioritised agenda of research gaps and future directions.

documents.abstract: This chapter provides an overview of emerging efforts to apply artificial intelligence (AI) to mental health assessment, including art-based assessment. As art therapy assessment requires ongoing, integrative, and attentive clinical judgment, the often opaque or “black box” nature of AI systems that analyze large datasets raises practical and ethical questions. The chapter reviews the feasibility, risks, and limitations of AI-enabled tools for art-based assessment and centers on a conversation with Taeeun Kim, an art therapist and researcher based in South Korea who contributed to the development of AI assessment applications for art therapy practice and education. Drawing on an in-depth interview with Kim, alongside established frameworks for evaluating AI tools in mental health, the chapter critically examines key ethical and clinical considerations. It concludes with practical recommendations and preliminary guidelines for art therapists and related professionals who may encounter, evaluate, or seek to develop AI-enabled assessment tools, with particular attention to protecting client agency, clinical judgment, cultural understanding, and contextual awareness.

documents.abstract: It covers how AI is used in networking by reviewing seven real survey papers, including machine learning techniques for solving networking problems, traffic classification and prediction for identifying and forecasting network traffic, intrusion detection for detecting cyberattacks, reinforcement learning for optimizing routing in software-defined networks, AI-native 6G networks for integrating intelligence into network design, and large language models for network management through natural-language configuration, troubleshooting, and diagnosis.

The article provides a comprehensive analysis of the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in cybersecurity, taking into account the latest technological trends of 2024–2026. The main possibilities of applying AI to protect information systems are studied: automatic detection of threats and anomalies, real-time incident response, prediction and prevention of cyberattacks, recognition of malicious code and phishing, and continuous learning and adaptation of defense systems. Particular attention is paid to the phenomenon of autonomous AI agents as a new stage in the evolution of intelligent cyber defense systems: practical cases of agentic incident triage and investigation systems (Microsoft Security Copilot), autonomous vulnerability discovery (Google Big Sleep), autonomous penetration testing (XBOW, PentestGPT), as well as the first documented case of an AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign are analyzed. The risks and challenges associated with the use of AI are considered: misuse of technologies by attackers, false positives and missed threats, vulnerabilities of machine learning models and agentic systems, and ethical and legal aspects. The necessity of a balanced approach combining automated AI systems with expert human control based on human-in-the-loop and human-on-the-loop models is substantiated.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied across finance, including fraud detection, risk assessment, and forecasting, yet forecasting and internal controls are often governed in separate initiatives. This paper examines two pillars of AI use in finance: AI-driven financial modeling and forecasting, and AI-driven reconciliation within internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). The paper is based on a literature review of 23 academic, regulatory, and standards sources, including materials from the SEC, PCAOB, and COSO. The review indicates that the two pillars are interdependent: reconciled, well-governed data underpins reliable forecasting, and continuous reconciliation combined with predictive modeling can support pre-filing risk detection in SEC reporting. Model risk management, explainability, and human sign-off emerge as governance requirements common to both pillars. Building on these insights, the paper proposes a five-stage maturity framework that sequences AI-driven reconciliation ahead of predictive forecasting, together with shared governance practices. The findings suggest that managing forecasting and controls under a unified governance approach offers a coherent pathway for AI adoption in finance. JEL classification numbers: C53, G17, G32, M41, M42. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence in Finance, Financial Analytics, Automated Reconciliation, Internal Controls, AI-Driven Finance.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping India’s financial services sector, with fintech (digital) lending emerging as a key area of adoption. Built on the country’s large-scale digital public infrastructure, digital lenders increasingly deploy AI across the credit lifecycle. These tools promise to widen formal credit access for new-to-credit and thin-file borrowers, micro and small enterprises, gig workers and low-to-mid-income households. However, they also raise concerns about algorithmic transparency, explainability, discrimination, consumer protection, privacy and cybersecurity. India has no single AI-specific law and oversight instead follows the sector-led, “techno-legal” approach set out in MeitY’s India AI Governance Guidelines (2025), which channels oversight through regulators such as the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). This report draws on structured interviews with industry leaders and technology vendors, together with a survey of 21 digital lending firms which are estimated to account for roughly 80% of digital lending volume in the country. The report maps trends in AI adoption, identifies operational and governance challenges, and assesses future trajectories. Firms see productivity gains but cannot yet attribute profitability to AI, which leaves the business case unproven even as investment intentions grow, particularly in collections and customer experience. The most significant risks are data quality, cybersecurity and dependence on third-party vendors. India relies on sector-led, principles-based oversight, and the RBI’s draft model risk guidance is not yet binding, so regulatory ambiguity persists. The central challenge is to extend governance outward to customers, vendors and data supply chains, as quickly as deployment advances.

documents.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning, natural language processing, and generative AI, is rapidly transforming medical education, particularly anatomy, assessment, and simulation.Objective: To systematically review the applications, educational benefits, limitations, ethical concerns, and emerging trends of AI in medical education since 2023.Methods: A structured literature search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and major medical-education publishers for studies published from January 2023 to July 2026.Twenty-nine eligible studies were synthesised across seven thematic domains.Results: AI applications included large language models, anatomy education tools, virtual simulation, AI-assisted assessment, and personalised learning.Evidence suggests potential benefits in learning support, simulation, question generation, and anatomy education.However, concerns regarding accuracy, hallucination, bias, academic integrity, privacy, and inadequate AI literacy remain.Evidence for improved educational outcomes is still limited, with many studies being small, single-centre, or pilot investigations.Conclusion: AI is becoming an important component of medical education, with particularly promising applications in anatomy and pre-clinical teaching.Responsible integration requires faculty oversight, competency-based AI literacy, ethical governance, validation of AI-generated educational content, and stronger outcome-based research.

documents.abstract: OBJECTIVES: We evaluated the transformative impact of AI modalities on clinical practice, distinguishing between retrospective algorithmic performance and prospective clinical effectiveness. METHODS: Comprehensive searches were executed [databases searched: January 2016 to October 2024] across PubMed/Medline, Scopus, and Web of Science, identifying peer-reviewed original research and clinical trials. Non-peer-reviewed materials and commercial web sources were strictly excluded. RESULTS: AI technologies-particularly deep learning (DL), natural language processing (NLP), and foundation models-demonstrate high diagnostic accuracy in retrospective cohorts across radiology, dermatology, and pathology. In precision therapeutics, AI accelerates drug discovery and facilitates multi-omics integration for individualized treatment planning. Furthermore, autonomous AI systems have proven cost-effective in nationwide diabetic retinopathy screening programs. However, significant gaps remain between in-silico success and real-world clinical utility. Primary barriers include the lack of prospective randomized trials, pervasive risks of algorithmic bias threatening health equity, the "black box" nature of deep neural networks, and stringent interoperability challenges. CONCLUSION: AI serves as a potent computational catalyst for advancing personalized medicine. To transition from retrospective experimental success to standard-of-care clinical integration, future research endeavors must prioritize Explainable AI (XAI), federated learning frameworks for privacy preservation, and rigorous prospective clinical validation under standardized regulatory oversight.

documents.abstract: This article examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in school counseling and argues that AI-based tools should support, rather than replace, the professional work of school counselors. Drawing on an analytical review of international policy documents, professional standards, empirical studies and the legislation of the Republic of Uzbekistan, the paper identifies four main areas of application: administrative and data-management support, academic and career guidance, early identification of students who may need help, and conversational agents for social-emotional support. Studies of mental health chatbots report short-term reductions in self-reported depressive symptoms among young adults; however, the overall quality of the evidence remains limited, safety has rarely been evaluated, and school-age children have seldom been studied. The article also discusses the key risks of AI use: breaches of confidentiality, algorithmic bias, inaccurate or harmful responses, and the weakening of the human relationship that lies at the core of counseling. Particular attention is paid to Uzbekistan, where the Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies until 2030 and the Law on Personal Data create both opportunities and obligations for schools. The paper concludes with practical principles for responsible use: human oversight, data protection, transparency, evidence-based tool selection, AI literacy for counselors, clear crisis protocols and linguistic and cultural adaptation.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence has shown strong performance on selected skin lesion classification tasks, but accurate image classification alone does not establish clinical benefit. Differences in data provenance, disease spectrum, evaluation design and human interaction complicate interpretation of published results. The main objective of the study was to critically examine representative evidence on artificial intelligence for skin cancer recognition, with emphasis on dermoscopic imaging, public datasets, diagnostic evaluation and clinical translation. A focused narrative synthesis was developed using targeted literature searches and verification of primary publications, dataset descriptors and reporting guidelines through 21 October 2026. This was not a systematic review or meta-analysis. No new model was trained and no patient-level data were analysed. Early retrospective studies established the feasibility of convolutional neural networks for selected diagnostic comparisons. Subsequent research demonstrated both potential benefits of clinician–AI collaboration and susceptibility to misleading support. Prospective multicentre evaluation provides stronger evidence of diagnostic performance, while showing clinically relevant sensitivity–specificity trade-offs. Public datasets support reproducibility but differ in imaging modality, diagnostic labels, reference standards and sampling. Class imbalance, related images across data partitions, skin-tone disparities, acquisition artifacts and distribution shift remain central concerns. Explanations may influence decisions differently depending on user expertise and the order of presentation. The evidence supports continued evaluation of AI as assistance for defined clinical tasks. Responsible translation requires independent validation, transparent reference standards, subgroup analysis, calibrated operating thresholds, and prospective measurement of patient and service outcomes. Comparative evaluation of the complete clinician–AI workflow should take priority over isolated claims of architectural superiority.

documents.abstract: The article examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in teaching English as a foreign language. It describes the main categories of AI tools currently used in language education, including large language model chatbots, automated writing evaluation systems, speech recognition applications, adaptive learning platforms and machine translation. On the basis of an analysis of international and Uzbek scholarly literature and normative documents, the article identifies how these tools can support the development of the four language skills, personalise learning and provide immediate feedback. At the same time, it discusses the risks associated with AI, such as factual inaccuracy, threats to academic integrity, data privacy concerns, excessive dependence on technology and unequal access. The authors argue that AI should complement rather than replace the teacher and offer practical recommendations for the responsible integration of AI into English lessons in the educational system of Uzbekistan.

The subject of research — features of application and development of artificial intelligence technologies, which are becoming key in the digital economy. The aim of the work is to determine the level and characteristics of development of artificial intelligence for different countries, as well as its dependence on the participation of state institutions and influence of constant generation of innovations. The article analyzes the state and structure of artificial intelligence market by different segments: by types of technologies, by deployment models, by solutions, by end-users, company size and geography. The work reveals the main trends of market development, identified and argued advantages and possible disadvantages of using these advanced technologies. The research methods include application of general science analysis and synthesis methods, classification and system, methods of grouping and comparison, economic analysis, as well as historical and comparative-legal methods. The results of the study showed that responsible adoption of artificial intelligence technologies becomes crucial for its positive impact on society. The growing demand for digital information technologies should lead to increased demands for accountability and transparency in the development of artificial intelligence technologies, to the development of a legal doctrine on its development at the international level. The findings of the study point to the need for proactive tools to regulate the legal framework of artificial intelligence, through which the process of developing and using artificial intelligence becomes dynamic and responsible, The use of artificial intelligence systems is synchronized with the global goals of social development.

Abstract Bacterial and fungal leaf diseases frequently produce overlapping visual symptoms, complicating automated diagnosis and limiting the transferability of models across crops and field conditions. This review systematically evaluates artificial intelligence methods for the morphology-based detection and differentiation of these diseases. Following a PRISMA-based selection process, 95 records published between 2017 and 2026 were identified, of which 59 eligible studies were included. The survey covers the morphological characteristics that distinguish bacterial and fungal diseases, traditional image processing and machine learning approaches, deep learning and generative AI techniques, and publicly available datasets. It also critically compares the performance, advantages, and limitations of existing diagnostic approaches. The findings indicate that deep learning dominates the literature, particularly in fungal disease detection, whereas research on bacterial diseases and generative AI applications remains comparatively limited. Although convolutional and transfer-learning models generally demonstrated strong classification performance, comparisons across studies were constrained by differences in datasets, evaluation protocols, and performance metrics. The principal barriers to practical adoption include morphological overlap between infections, class imbalance, and scarcity of expert-annotated images of bacterial and early-stage diseases, reliance on controlled-background datasets, limited external validation, model complexity, and insufficient interpretability. Future research should prioritize pathogen-balanced multicrop field datasets, standardized reporting and cross-dataset evaluation, multimodal fusion of RGB images with spectral and environmental data, domain adaptation, validated generative augmentation, explainable models, and lightweight edge deployment. By connecting lesion morphology with methodological and dataset evidence, this review provides a structured roadmap for developing robust, interpretable, and field-ready plant disease diagnosis systems.

documents.abstract: Farm workers operating in sugarcane fields, forests, tea plantations, and other areas with thick vegetation may encounter hazardous animals and insects that are difficult to notice before approaching them. Conventional precautions, including sticks, torches, protective footwear, and visual observation, offer limited capability for identifying concealed threats in advance. Delays in communication and access to medical assistance can further increase the risks associated with such incidents. Recent progress in Artificial Intelligence (AI), computer vision, thermal imaging, edge computing, Global Positioning System (GPS) technology, and the Internet of Things (IoT) provides opportunities to develop wearable systems for improved agricultural safety. This paper presents a focused narrative review of research relevant to an AI-enabled safety cap, covering animal recognition, snake detection, thermal-based wildlife monitoring, edge deployment, and IoT- supported alert systems. The reviewed approaches are discussed across three areas: sensing methods, including visible-light cameras, thermal sensors, and supplementary positioning or motion sensors; deep-learning techniques, including YOLO -based detectors, transformer architectures, lightweight models, and object tracking; and system designs combining local processing, offline data handling, and cloud connectivity. Published results indicate that some animal and snake detection models achieve approximately 92–98% on selected evaluation metrics, while one thermal wildlife detection approach reports 89.1% mAP50 with approximately 1.45 million parameters. Certain lightweight YOLOv8 models have also demonstrated processing rates of around 52–65 frames per second on Jetson -class hardware, although performance may vary across devices and experimental settings. Despite these advances, much of the existing research relies on fixed cameras, aerial platforms, or controlled datasets. Limitations include restricted species coverage, insufficiently documented datasets partitioning, and limited evaluation under real agricultural conditions. The reviewed evidence does not establish the field performance of an integrated, multi-camera, head-worn safety device incorporating behaviour analysis, battery endurance assessment, and emergency alert testing. To address these gaps, this paper outlines a conceptual worker-to-cloud architecture combining visual and thermal sensing, edge-based inference, multi modal warnings, optional GPS-enabled SOS communication, and systematic field evaluation. The review also identifies research priorities for developing a practical and reliable wearable safety solution for agricultural workers.

Nanomedicine is a promising strategy for cancer therapy. However, the low delivery efficiency of nanoparticles (NPs) to tumors remains a challenge and hinders clinical translation. In this study, an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model was developed to predict NPs' tumor delivery efficiency (DE) based on the physicochemical properties and experimental strategies. First, a generic PBPK model was applied to describe NPs’ tumor kinetics, and six different tumor-related parameters were determined. Second, machine learning (ML) and AI models were developed for predicting the tumor-related parameters. Incorporating the ML-predicted parameters into the PBPK model, an ML-assisted PBPK model was developed to predict the tumor kinetics of NPs. This generic PBPK model was applied to simulate the tumor kinetics, in which 114 out of 152 datasets (75%) achieved the determination coefficient (R 2 ) of ≥0.75, and the overall R 2 was 0.92. Distribution (PT) and permeability (PATC) coefficients at the tumor site were the most important parameters in predicting tumor DEs. The deep neural network (DNN) model was the best-performing model and selected for tumor-related parameter estimations. Targeting strategy and surface charge were determined as the important features for predicting various tumor-related PBPK parameters. External validation was conducted using an in vivo experiment, and half of the predicted concentrations were within the two-fold error of the observed data. This model can serve as a complementary tool for predicting tumor kinetics prior to animal experimentation, helping identify promising NP formulations and potentially improving the success rate of drug delivery.

This paper addresses AI-based cell sleep scheduling for dense 5G/6G radio access networks, where the central challenge is reducing energy consumption without degrading delay, blocking probability, or switching stability. The literature indicates growing interest in 3GPP and O-RAN energy-saving control, but many existing methods rely on local traffic thresholds or RL agents with weak spatial awareness. To address this gap, the paper proposes Graph-Aware Multi-Objective Sleep Scheduling (GMOSS), which combines graph neural encoding of inter-cell coupling with a dueling double DQN and a safety layer that filters overload-prone actions. Unlike generic GNN-RL controllers, GMOSS formulates cell sleep scheduling as a topology-aware constrained decision problem in which graph encoding, multi-objective value learning, and safety-constrained action projection are jointly used to prevent overload-prone sleep decisions before execution. A dense heterogeneous network with 19 cells is simulated under diurnal non-stationary traffic. Compared with Always-On, threshold control, independent DQN, and multi-agent DQN baselines, the proposed method achieves the best energy–QoS trade-off. Across 30 randomized seeds, GMOSS reduces average RAN power by 31.8% versus Always-On and 18.6% versus threshold control, improves energy efficiency to 1.058 Mbit/J, lowers blocking to 1.84%, and reduces switches per hour to 4.3. The gain in energy efficiency over independent DQN is 11.2% with a 95% confidence interval of [8.7%, 13.6%] and p < 0.001. The contribution of the paper lies in explicitly coupling spatial coordination, wake-up cost awareness, and practical safety constraints in a single AI controller that is well aligned with O-RAN style deployment.

documents.abstract: Abstract Despite the vast growth of artificial intelligence (AI) in chemical research, educational programs have struggled to keep pace in familiarizing and preparing students for its implementation. In response to this gap, we have developed an interdisciplinary experiment for senior undergraduate and postgraduate students to discuss the implementations of AI in analytical chemistry with a focus on sensing. For this, an example paper-based fluorescent sensor was employed for the detection of H2O2 using image-based signal readout and machine learning-based concentration quantification. The Horseradish Peroxidase (HRP)-catalyzed yellow fluorescence emission resulting from the interaction of ortho-phenylenediamine (OPD) with H2O2 was recorded using smartphone cameras. Various features were extracted from the images and used to develop machine learning models for quantifying H2O2 concentration. Through this experiment, an introduction to sensing and paper-based sensor development, as well as the implementation of AI in sensor data analysis, was presented. During the lab experiment, students successfully developed Artificial Neural Network (ANN) models, validated them, and optimized them to improve performance. The feedback showed that students had become familiar with AI and machine learning and had increased interest in using AI in their future research.

This critical review synthesizes empirical studies of algorithmically personalized and artificial-intelligence-generated music interventions reporting neurophysiological, neuroimaging, or objective behavioral outcomes. Literature was identified through structured searches of PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library through 12 August 2026, with CNKI and Wanfang searched on 22 September 2026, supplemented by citation tracking. Twenty-one eligible studies (at least 1,005 participants) were identified. Five things the term artificial intelligence covers in this literature are separated: algorithmic selection from a corpus, rule-based sonification, parametric modulation of pre-existing material, machine-learning generative composition, and closed-loop delivery contingent on the listener’s own signal. Only three studies used a machine-learning generative model, so most of the evidence concerns algorithmic personalization of existing material. Studies of closed-loop neural systems reported the most consistent neurophysiological signal, and music-based alpha neurofeedback produced higher normalized alpha power than yoked random feedback. In an open-loop design, personalized EEG-derived music was reported to attenuate anxiety induction where self-selected preferred music and silence did not, with enhanced prefrontal theta oscillations as the associated correlate. Eight studies carried a comparator capable of isolating an algorithmic component from music exposure, and all eight favored the algorithmic condition. These eight address different causal questions, use different designs, and point to no single mechanism, so their results are best read as preliminary and hypothesis-generating. Evidence quality was very low throughout. The median reported sample size was 22, no study blinded participants or measured expectancy, and no specific finding has been independently replicated. GRADE certainty was very low for every outcome domain, covering EEG oscillatory power, sleep architecture, autonomic regulation, epileptiform activity, and cognitive, behavioral and affective outcomes. Neurophysiological change is reported more often than behavioral change, and behavioral change more often than clinical benefit. The evidence supports continued investigation and does not support clinical deployment. Eight reporting and design requirements for future trials are proposed.

topics: Adsorption and biosorption for pollutant removal

documents.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with Lean, Six Sigma and Lean Six Sigma (LSS) and develop a conceptual framework for AI-enabled operational excellence. Design/methodology/approach A combined bibliometric and thematic review was conducted using 52 Scopus-indexed journal articles. Publication trends, co-authorship, keyword co-occurrence, citation patterns and bibliographic coupling were integrated with qualitative thematic synthesis. Findings The field has progressed from Lean–Industry 4.0 alignment toward AI-enabled process improvement, LSS4.0, digitally enhanced define–measure–analyze–improve–control and decision intelligence. Five themes emerged: Lean digital transformation, AI-supported Six Sigma, LSS4.0 integration, AI-enabled decision intelligence and sustainability-oriented performance. Research limitations/implications The Scopus-only journal corpus may exclude relevant contributions. Future studies should empirically validate the framework and examine sector-specific applications and human–AI collaboration. Practical implications The framework guides organizations in aligning data infrastructure, AI capabilities, improvement routines, workforce competencies, leadership and governance when developing AI-enabled LSS systems. Social implications Responsible integration may support resource efficiency, sustainability, workforce development, transparency and accountability in AI-supported improvement decisions. Originality/value This study consolidates fragmented research into an evidence-informed framework connecting digital infrastructure, AI capability, process-improvement logic, organizational enablement and governance and value realization.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This study introduces the concept of computer communication spillover: the transfer of interaction patterns from human–computer to human–human contexts via cue-triggered habit activation. The possibility of such transfer is supported by theories of power, habit formation, and social practice. Human interaction with large language models (LLMs) is here presented as a theoretical example, where the compliant nature of LLMs is central to the argument. We argue that by repeatedly occupying a superior, controlling position, LLM users may develop directive, instrumental, and control-oriented communication habits. Such habits might spill over to human-human communication contexts, where they could reduce politeness, tolerance for dissent, and openness to other people' perspectives. Because habits typically develop gradually, outside users’ awareness, spillover effects can raise ethical-legal questions about responsibility and human agency. Overall, we propose that computer communication spillover might be a broader societal risk of generative AI.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Large language models produce assertion-shaped outputs that often bring their users to true belief. I argue for two conclusions of different strengths: that on the best current evidence, these systems do not transmit testimonial knowledge and that hearers are not now positioned to accord their outputs testimonial uptake, which does not wait on the first. From Burge, Williamson, Goldberg, Faulkner, and Lackey, I derive a Tracking Minimum: a source transmits testimonial knowledge that p only if the truth of p , or the evidential support for p , figures in the explanation of its producing that assertion, and does so in virtue of the source’s own production process rather than of a proxy on which that process depends. It is this endogeneity requirement, not any modal profile, that the five accounts share and current systems fail. The argument engages Burge’s extension of his framework to computational sources, the interpretability literature, and the published case for AI testimony, whose dispute with mine turns on an empirically decidable question, for which an experiment is specified. The positive proposal places LLM outputs within an extended epistemology of instruments, with a result that has gone unremarked: a working barometer satisfies the condition these systems fail.

PURPOSE: This study aimed to map the development of assistive and adaptive technology-supported approaches to dyscalculia between 2005 and 2025 and to clarify how artificial intelligence, adaptive learning, and assistive technologies are positioned within this research field. METHODS: A bibliometric review, complemented by a narrative synthesis, was conducted using 83 unique journal publications indexed in Web of Science and Scopus. The analysis included keyword frequency analysis, title-term distribution, keyword co-occurrence networks, thematic mapping, thematic evolution, and country-level collaboration analysis. RESULTS: The findings show that early research was largely grounded in neurocognitive explanations of dyscalculia, particularly numerical processing, working memory, and developmental learning difficulties. Recent publications indicate a broadening towards digital interventions, adaptive learning environments, serious games, augmented reality applications, and AI-supported assistive technologies. Studies using machine learning, deep learning, and probabilistic models suggest potential uses of AI for early screening, personalised feedback, individualised support, and cognitive support. However, AI remains an emerging rather than fully central organising theme. The review identified international collaboration patterns across Asia, the Middle East, Europe, and North America, alongside methodological and ethical issues, including limited longitudinal evidence, variability in intervention designs, biases in database and keyword selection, data privacy, and algorithmic transparency. CONCLUSIONS: Technology-assisted dyscalculia research has expanded from cognitive and developmental explanations towards more intervention-oriented, adaptive, and assistive technology-informed approaches. AI-supported assistive technologies appear promising for early identification, accessibility, individualised learning support, and participation in mathematics-related activities, but require stronger empirical validation, ethical implementation, user-centred evaluation, and integration into educational and rehabilitation-related support contexts.
topics: Cognitive and developmental aspects of mathematical skills
Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: BACKGROUND: Dental assistants are often susceptible to musculoskeletal disorders due to their professional duties; however, data on ergonomic risks for them are limited. AIM: To compare the severity of pain syndrome in dental assistants while working on chairs of different designs. METHODS: The study involved eight dental assistants who worked for two months on chairs of various designs and subjectively assessed pain severity using the visual analog scale (VAS). Before the start of each work shift, each assistant received one of two types of dental chair using a random number generator: a chair with armrests or a chair without armrests. Randomization was conducted independently for each shift and each participant. The resulting 221 observations were divided into two groups depending on the type of chair used during the shift: group 1 included 106 measurements obtained after a shift on a chair without armrests, and group 2 included 115 measurements obtained after a shift on a chair with armrests. Statistical analysis included assessment of normality of distribution (Shapiro–Wilk test), group comparisons (Student t-test, Mann–Whitney U test), and ROC analysis. Differences were considered statistically significant at p ≤ 0.05. RESULTS: Neck pain was the most common symptom in dental assistants (70%). Shoulder pain ranked second in frequency (52% of cases), and upper back pain ranked third (35%). When working on a chair with armrests, the median pain severity on the VAS was significantly lower in the neck (3.0 vs 5.0 points; p 0.001), right (3.0 vs 5.0 points; p 0.001) and left (2.5 vs 5.0 points; p 0.001) shoulders, as well as in the upper back on the right (4.0 vs 5.0 points; p = 0.030). For the upper back on the left, the differences did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.086). ROC analysis showed the best predictive ability of the model for the shoulders (AUC = 0.802 on the right; AUC = 0.804 on the left), moderate for the neck (AUC = 0.739–0.745) and the upper back on the right (AUC = 0.705). CONCLUSION: When comparing the groups, work on a chair with armrests was characterized by lower pain severity in the neck, shoulders, and upper back on the right than work on chairs of other designs.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Purpose Radon is a radioactive gas that produces a large amount of alpha particles during its decay process and a well-recognized health hazard, particularly an established risk factor for lung cancer in high-risk populations such as miners. Although hematological and biochemical parameters are useful indicators of human health status, the impact of radon exposure on these parameters among male miners remains unclear.Methods The participants of this study are 283 male miners in a tin mine in China. A targeted research design was adopted to conduct a questionnaire survey, physical examination, blood sample analysis coupled with radon concentration measurements, statistical analysis was performed to investigate the impact of varying levels of radon exposure on hematological and biochemical parameters among the participants.Results Mean platelet volume (MPV), plateletcrit (PCT), and platelet-large cell ratio (P-LCR) decreased significantly across the working-level month (WLM) groups (Bonferroni-corrected P < 0.003), as did albumin (ALB) and the albumin-to-globulin (A/G) ratio (Bonferroni-corrected P < 0.0045). In contrast, urea and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) increased significantly (Bonferroni-corrected P < 0.0045), whereas platelet count did not differ significantly among groups. Multiple linear regression confirmed WLM as an independent predictor for MPV (β= −0.282, P < 0.0001), PCT (β= −0.165, P = 0.010), P-LCR (β= −0.206, P = 0.002), urea (β = 0.178, P = 0.008), and platelet distribution width (β = 0.184, P = 0.006). All values remained within clinically normal reference ranges.Conclusion Cumulative occupational radon exposure was independently associated with decreased platelet volume indices and elevated urea levels in miners, suggesting subclinical hematological changes and altered renal-related parameters. MPV may serve as a candidate indicator requiring further validation of radiation-related hematopoietic alterations. These findings contribute to occupational health surveillance frameworks for populations chronically exposed to radon in mining environments.

Language-model agents acquire capability along two routes that published work almost always varies together, one enlarging the computation a single agent performs and the other enlarging the number of agents and the channels along which they pass partial results, which leaves the contribution of each route indistinguishable. This paper separates an agent system into a reasoning operator and an interaction topology, holding the number of agents fixed at three across all multi-agent topologies, together with the number of rounds, the message cap, the prompt skeleton, and the memory settings for all combinations, and evaluates a full factorial design of four reasoning levels and four topologies on three public test sets totalling 484 instances under five random seeds, giving 38,720 task executions. Comparisons are paired at the instance level, and effects are estimated from logistic mixed-effects models fitted to each test set separately. The reasoning factor spans 18.0 points on the static suite whereas the topology factor spans 7.8 points on the interactive one, a reversal indicating that the two mechanisms act on different failure modes. The topology span is taken across all four topology levels and therefore includes the step from one agent to three, against a structure-only span of 2.8 points among the multi-agent topologies. The two factors also depart from additivity in a localised manner. A mechanism-motivated single-degree-of-freedom contrast on the only cell in which both factors contribute a corrective pass is significant at p = 0.001 on the static suite, whereas the omnibus nine-degree-of-freedom interaction test is not (p = 0.094), and in that cell the observed 50.0 percent lies 5.8 points below the additive expectation. After tokens are counted, seven of the sixteen configurations remain undominated on the static suite and five on the operating-system suite, and returns saturate at 12,400 tokens per instance on the static suite under the present design.

The enormous amount of data that arrives daily from our personal gadgets, massive company networks, and cloud services has, in fact, caused a crisis for digital forensics. The conventional manual investigational methods, which were designed for a one-device-at-a-time world, cannot be used anymore. The “scaling problem” is not only about the number of cases but also about their complexity. In fact, investigators nowadays are having to face several terabytes of data; however, these are not only scattered across various cloud servers but are also encrypted and exist in a multitude of formats. The data is being produced and is changing at a very high speed, and at the same time, there is a strong and urgent demand to deliver the results quickly, which has, therefore, put forensic teams under enormous pressure and is, in fact, at the verge of a breaking point. The discipline is turning to automation, artificial intelligence (AI), and current computing frameworks in order to get out of this data blockade. The goal is to employ these technologies to perform those parts of the investigation that are extremely laborious, time-consuming, and tedious, such as data collection and filtering. Consequently, human analysts are freed from routine tasks and can therefore devote themselves to work with the most critical evidence. This transformation is facilitating the development of the new generation of forensic platforms, such as Autonomous Forensic Systems (AFS), which are designed for continuous monitoring and intelligent, adaptive decision-making. This paper discusses how the scaling problem has led digital forensics to change its way of working and how AI and cloud computing are increasingly becoming indispensable to the viability of investigations in our world, which is overloaded with data.

Understanding language-agent behaviour requires learning how actions are organised across a trajectory and how this organisation relates to context and outcomes. We propose a general framework that connects data-driven behavioural discovery with analysis and experimental investigation. Categories developed from recorded activity define what is measured. Analyses preserve the behaviours' positions in the process and express their relationships as interpretable hypotheses. Statistical assessment and tests in held-out contexts examine the strength and scope of the evidence. Experiments, including prompt steering, then test how behaviour and outcomes change under deliberately varied conditions. A study of iterative self-reflection illustrates how discovery, dependency learning and prompt comparisons can inform one another. We develop this approach for trajectories of varying length, event order and agent roles, and identify advances in coding, analysis and experimentation needed to support its wider use.

Generative AI (GenAI) is shifting software engineering students' work from producing artefacts towards evaluating and supervising AI-generated outputs. However, little is known about what characteristics students identify in outputs when reporting interventions, or how they exercise oversight during authentic software engineering work. We analysed 962 student-AI interaction turns documented by 145 first-year software engineering students through structured AI Journals, including 172 student-declared interventions. Using a multi-dimensional coding framework, we characterised the output characteristics identified in these reported interventions, students' reasons for intervening, the actions they took, and how those actions were enacted. Fitness problems were identified in 74.4% of interventions, compared with 16.9% involving correctness problems, indicating that oversight more often concerned whether plausible AI outputs were suitable for the engineering task than whether they contained explicit errors. Among classifiable interventions, students most frequently modified generated outputs (51.0%) or refined their prompts (28.2%), with both response types commonly associated with engineering fit. Within-student analysis further showed that outputs perceived as containing minor flaws were associated with lower evaluation confidence than outputs perceived as perfect. Taken together, these findings characterise novice AI oversight as a process that extends beyond error detection to encompass both judgement of fitness for purpose and active intervention in AI-assisted engineering work.

Existing evaluation protocols for unit tests rely on aggregate metrics such as branch coverage and mutation score. These metrics quantify the extent to which a test suite exercises program behavior, but do not identify the behavioral obligations it systematically leaves unchecked. We propose BlindSpotEval, an obligation-based evaluation framework aligned with the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern. The framework comprises three metrics, Boundary-Value Adequacy, Control-Flow Adequacy, and Oracle Strength, complemented by an assessment of execution reliability. We also introduce ObligBench, a complexity-stratified Java benchmark comprising 895 complex and 700 low-complexity functions with source-side obligation annotations. Evaluating 14,320 tests from four LLMs under four prompting strategies reveals systematic blind spots. Incorrect assertions account for 15.6% of test failures, illustrating that coverage alone does not establish oracle correctness. Among executable tests, coverage of null, negative, and empty arguments reaches only 34.8%, 23.8%, and 38.8%, compared with average coverage above 93% for booleans. Catch blocks and default groups have Control-Flow Adequacy scores of only 0.100 and 0.312. Across both dimensions, LLM-generated tests exhibit the happy-path bias observed in human-written tests, concentrating on normal inputs and expected flows while leaving unusual values and exceptional paths unchecked. Oracle strength is high on average but uneven, with weaker assertions for object return property values and exceptions. These blind spots also occur in low-complexity functions, suggesting that code complexity alone does not explain them. BlindSpotEval provides construct-level adequacy profiles that identify under-tested obligation types and can guide targeted improvements beyond those supported by aggregate scores alone.

Large language models often acquire specialized capabilities through successive pretraining stages, but these gains can come at the cost of forgetting earlier knowledge. In this work, we investigate whether such trade-offs can be improved by changing how strongly each domain contributes to learning while keeping its data exposure fixed. We find that, in controlled knowledge--mathematics experiments, loss reweighting produces a single checkpoint that surpasses the best knowledge and reasoning scores attained along either stage trajectory. This reveals an independent control that data-mixture ratios alone do not capture. Building on this finding, we propose LARE (Loss-Adaptive Reweighting under fixed Exposure), which automatically adjusts domain weights from running loss statistics. Motivated by a theoretical analysis of gradient noise, its normalized inverse-square-root rule balances relative loss scales without changing the sampled mixture or requiring additional runs to search for weights. Across knowledge, mathematics, and code, \Method{} improves all five evaluated benchmarks for a 1.5B model trained on 240B tokens, averaging +7.84 pp over a matched direct mixture, including gains of +17.06 pp on GSM8K and +9.00 pp on MATH. These findings demonstrate that adjusting domain loss scales can improve joint capabilities without additional domain exposure.

LLM agents retrieve skills from public hubs that hold up to about 100,000 entries and serve many models. As models improve, a hub must find the skills a given model has internalized, meaning it can do without them, and retire them for that model, yet internalization has not been measured with known reliability. Published rules that compare runs with and without a skill retire on the gain alone. The gain is near zero both for an internalized skill and when neither the model nor the skill delivers the capability, a state we call uncovered. We instead withhold the skill, score the model on a task synthesized from it, and trust a high unaided score only when another model gains from the skill, since nearly half of high scores come from tasks no model benefits from. Under four models, a published gain rule applied with one task per skill removes over half of the uncovered skills. On SkillsBench, 28 of its 31 retirements rest on probes no run passed in full, while retiring on the unaided score costs no detectable reward. Unaided verdicts reproduce across tasks more often than the gain rule's (Cohen's kappa 0.42 against 0.23) but differ across models, so a hub must read them per model. We release 1,251 skills with tasks and item scores under four models.

Purpose This study examines how anthropomorphic cues that make AI agency socially salient influence employee work engagement in mandatory, performance-oriented human–AI collaboration. It distinguishes AI agency from AI anthropomorphism, tests affective and evaluative motivational mechanisms and identifies perceived AI threat as a boundary condition grounded in the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model. Design/methodology/approach Across two pilot studies and two main experiments (total N = 501), we used immersive workplace role-playing scenarios to test a dual-pathway model. Integrating social response theory with the JD-R model, this research tests a dual-pathway model in which anthropomorphic design influences work engagement through emotional bonding and acquisitive impression management motive (IMM), whereas perceived artificial intelligence threat operates as a hindrance demand that weakens these resource pathways. Findings Anthropomorphic AI enhanced work engagement through two motivational routes: an affective route via emotional bonding and an evaluative route via IMM. However, perceived AI threat significantly attenuated these benefits. When threat was high, the positive effects of anthropomorphism on emotional bonding, IMM and work engagement became non-significant, suggesting that replacement-related threat drains the psychological capacity needed for anthropomorphic cues to function as job resources. Originality/value This research contributes to workplace AI and information systems (IS) scholarship by clarifying how anthropomorphic cues make AI agency socially salient without equating anthropomorphism with agency. It extends prior work on anthropomorphic AI and engagement by identifying an evaluative pathway – performing for AI – alongside the affective pathway of bonding with AI. It also offers a contingency-based explanation for the anthropomorphism paradox by showing that the benefits of humanlike design depend on the surrounding AI-threat climate.

Purpose We examine how types of secondary activities relate to primary job performance under bounded rationality and when managers should permit, encourage, or restrict them. Design/methodology/approach Using an archival dataset from professional baseball (1945–2018), we classify secondary activities as unrelated, teaching-related, or learning-related. We estimate Ordinary Least Squares and difference-in-differences models around the 1965 Major League Baseball (MLB) draft and measure performance with Wins Above Replacement Findings Unrelated and teaching-related secondary activities are associated with lower performance, whereas learning-related secondary activities are associated with higher performance than teaching-related secondary activities. When the job becomes more salient, these negative associations intensify, while the performance advantage of learning-related secondary activities widens. Research limitations/implications Evidence derives from a single industry and an observational setting. The cognitively aligned typology and boundary-condition logic refine Behavioral Theory of the Firm accounts of attention allocation and offer testable extensions. Practical implications Rather than adopting blanket rules, managers should evaluate secondary activities according to their cognitive demands, intensity, alignment with the focal role, and demonstrated performance consequences, and revisit these evaluations as the stakes of the primary role rise. Social implications Differentiated policies, coupled with equitable skill-building alternatives, can enhance worker wellbeing while protecting core performance. Originality/value We move beyond the “secondary activity versus no secondary activity” view by testing a cognitively aligned typology and its moderators, translating Behavioral Theory of the Firm into actionable policy guidance.

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) connect language understanding with image-based reasoning and are increasingly explored as artificial intelligence systems for ophthalmic image analysis, workflow support, research prototyping, and education. This scoping review synthesizes 21 peer-reviewed studies that moved beyond text-only question answering to evaluate visual question answering (VQA), domain-adapted or fine-tuned ophthalmic models, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and low- or no-code tools for analytics and prototype development. Across studies, the evidence suggests early feasibility for image-conditioned explanations, triage support, documentation assistance, structured data extraction, and rapid tool creation. However, the evidence base remains heterogeneous and preliminary, with mixed diagnostic performance, variable prompts and model versions, limited external validation, and persistent risks including reasoning errors, hallucinations, session variability, privacy concerns, and security threats. To illustrate potential workflows not yet fully covered by the literature, we also provide clearly labeled author-built demonstrations, which are non-evidentiary, for fundus and optical coherence tomography (OCT)-based VQA, optical character recognition (OCR) tabulation, code-free analytics, automated software programming, and web-based risk calculators. Future priorities include extending image-conditioned reasoning to additional ophthalmic modalities, strengthening RAG with curated corpora and provenance, evaluating few-shot and in-context learning for rare conditions, and using controlled generative imaging for education and data augmentation. Overall, MLLMs may support supervised ophthalmic artificial intelligence applications in selected clinical, research, and educational workflows. Clinical deployment will require external validation, prospective human-in-the-loop evaluation, standards-based workflow integration, privacy-preserving infrastructure, audit logging, cybersecurity, and post-deployment monitoring.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping urban development across the Global South, offering opportunities to improve planning, public services, and resource management. However, AI-enabled systems operate within existing inequalities in infrastructure, representation, institutional capacity, and digital participation. This article argues that digital access alone is insufficient for inclusive urban AI. Drawing on data-justice scholarship and illustrative cases, it examines how AI can create uneven opportunities and risks for vulnerable populations. It calls for a context-sensitive approach that prioritises representative data, meaningful participation, accountability, human oversight, and safeguarding, ensuring that technological innovation contributes to more inclusive and equitable urban development outcomes.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become a persistent layer of work and learning rather than an occasional tool. Users must repeatedly decide when to delegate, how to prompt, whether to trust, how to verify, and how responsibility should be distributed. This integrative review defines AI fatigue as a cumulative reduction in the cognitive, affective, or motivational capacity for adaptive AI engagement when interaction, evaluation, correction, learning, and role-adjustment demands accumulate faster than recovery and support. The review connects technostress, automation vigilance, cognitive load and offloading, trust calibration, digital fatigue, and the Job Demands–Resources perspective. It introduces an Exposure–Adaptation–Depletion–Response framework, a five-domain taxonomy, and an AI Fatigue Load model that separates use volume from uncertainty, task stakes, correction burden, interruption, role disruption, and imposed adoption velocity. The analysis is updated to incorporate a 2026 validated 15-item AI Fatigue Scale; the proposed load model complements that psychophysiological outcome measure by specifying socio-technical antecedents and exposure conditions. Educational and organizational applications show why AI may simultaneously improve output and worsen human sustainability. The article identifies recurring inferential errors, presents a measurement and longitudinal research agenda, and proposes an intervention hierarchy spanning interface design, workflow, curriculum, organizational policy, and governance. AI fatigue is positioned neither as generic screen tiredness nor as a synonym for burnout, but as an adaptation problem located in the coupled human–AI–institution system.

This study utilized a quantitative descriptive-survey and correlational-predictive research design to systematically examine the variables dictating the college preferences of graduating senior high school learners. Conducted at Mindanao State University - Lanao National College of Arts and Trades (MSU-LNCAT) during the School Year 2025–2026, the investigation relied on a total seventy-three Grade 12 learner-respondents comprising of forty-three Humanities and Social Sciences Learner-respondents (58.90%) and thirty TVL track learner-respondents (41.10%), with a demographic concentration of fifty-six females (76.71%) and seventeen males (23.29%). Data was gathered via face-to-face classroom administration using a structured 5-point Likert scale questionnaire evaluating three predictive dimensions: Intrinsic Motivation, Familial Influence, and Peer Dynamics and Social Media Influence. Descriptive and inferential statistical treatments was used including frequency, percentage, weighted mean, standard deviation, item ranking, and the Pearson (r) Correlation Coefficient. Intrinsic Motivation emerged as the primary driver, yielding a high composite mean of 3.92 (High Influence) and a Significant Strong Positive Relationship, with course preferences, successfully rejecting the null hypothesis. Conversely, external factors had minimal impact; Familial Influence acted strictly as a secondary, consultative reference point with a neutral composite mean of 3.39 (Moderate Influence) and a weak, variable correlation, while Peer Dynamics and Social Media Influence exerted the weakest pressure, finishing with a low composite mean of 2.68 (Low Influence) and No Significant Relationship. Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that modern Grade 12 learner-respondents at MSU-LNCAT exercise high psychological autonomy, systematically prioritizing internal passion and specialized tracking competencies over parental expectations, peer circles, or digital trends.
keywords: technical and vocational education and training

documents.abstract: Participating in a conversation involves not only deciding what to say but also whether to speak at all. This judgment carries even greater significance in environments like the Werewolf game, where participants' interests conflict, because both utterances and silence are subject to interpretation and assessment by others. Therefore, determining when to speak, as well as what to say, is crucial for an LLM agent playing the Werewolf game. In this study, we introduce a Werewolf AI agent developed for the Anytime Utterance Track of the AIWolfDial shared task. Our system builds on the existing Inner Thoughts framework, which determines utterance timing during conversations by generating internal thoughts and evaluating the value of each thought for expression at that moment. Since existing methods were designed for general dialogue, we have redesigned the system specifically for the competitive environment and incomplete information setting of Werewolf games. We call our adapted method Adversarial Inner Thoughts. Through experiments involving analysis of self-play logs and human evaluations, we analyze and discuss the effectiveness of our approach.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Big Data and artificial intelligence are changing digital marketing through consumer behavior analysis, personalized communication, and automation. This paper examines their role in marketing processes, performance measurement, and the conditions for application in Serbia. A narrative review of selected literature is combined with a descriptive analysis of published statistics on ICT use, e-commerce, and enterprise AI adoption. The analysis identifies widespread consumer participation in digital channels alongside more limited enterprise adoption of AI. Serbia remains below the EU average in enterprise AI use, although above some member states. The paper’s contribution lies in linking data resources, analytical capabilities, and managerial competencies to explain why technology adoption alone is insufficient for effective digital marketing. Practical implications emphasize employee development, responsible data management, and the evaluation of marketing outcomes. The findings should be interpreted within the limits of aggregate indicators, which do not directly measure marketing-specific AI use or its effectiveness. Future research should examine these applications and their outcomes at the enterprise level.

Generative AI is increasingly embedded in team-based design, yet little is known about how teams negotiate its role over extended projects. We conducted a four-week situated study with nine graduate design teams (54 students) developing complete murder mystery Live Action Role-Playing games. Using domestication theory as a sensitizing framework, we analyzed 104 human-AI collaboration events, project outputs, and 27 semi-structured interviews. We identified three collaboration modes: Task-Based Empowered Creation, AI-Augmented Creative Co-creation, and Progressive Trust-Informed Collaboration. A fourth mode, Ceding Executive Trust Collaboration, was theoretically possible but did not occur. Across teams, AI was delegated tactical tasks such as content and asset generation, while humans retained control over narrative direction, quality standards, and core mechanics. We conceptualize this pattern as bounded delegation within a strategic-tactical hierarchy, offering an alternative to linear autonomy-progression models and informing AI tools that support rather than supplant human strategic control.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: HPC clusters are shared among many projects, each holding an allocation of node-hours, and ensuring fairness is becoming harder. Foundation models workflows and automated pipelines have made job submissions bursty and concentrated among a few heavy users, so occasional users absorb queueing delays created by frequent ones, with no indication of how long their jobs will wait. Existing schedulers either forget past usage, protect only the job at the head of the queue, or assume that running jobs can be preempted. We propose HyDRA, a Hybrid Deadline and Ranking-Aware scheduler that enforces fairness among users while bounding the queue wait of every job. HyDRA assigns each job a deadline on arrival based on its size, the priorities of its project and user, the current backlog, and how far its project and user are from their entitled share. It ranks waiting jobs by a priority score that grows with waiting time, serves jobs close to their deadlines first, and backfills a job only when no deadline, or fairness limit is violated.
