documents.abstract: Automated government case management is moving from digitised workflow toward intelligent triage, eligibility assessment, risk prioritisation and service routing. In Saudi Arabia, this transition is especially consequential because digital government programmes increasingly connect high-volume public services with data-intensive decision processes. The central challenge is not simply whether artificial intelligence can accelerate case handling, but whether decisions can remain timely, reviewable, understandable and contestable when models operate at operational speed. This review examines how explainable artificial intelligence and real-time decisioning can be combined for automated government case management in Saudi Arabia. It synthesises thirty DOI-verified studies published from 2020 to 2025 across explainability, human-AI decision support, public-sector algorithmic governance, Saudi digital government and streaming analytics. The review develops a socio-technical framework in which case intake, data quality, machine reasoning, rule validation, explanation generation, human oversight, notification, appeal and continuous monitoring form one auditable decision loop. The analysis finds that explainability is valuable only when it is matched to the decision recipient and linked to operational controls; generic feature-attribution displays alone do not guarantee justified or trustworthy outcomes. Real-time systems also require explicit latency budgets, uncertainty handling, concept-drift monitoring and escalation rules so that speed does not suppress due process. For Saudi public agencies, successful adoption depends on combining interoperable data, secure governance, accountable ownership and Arabic-capable explanation interfaces with measurable human override and appeal mechanisms. The study proposes evaluation criteria spanning predictive validity, explanation fidelity, decision latency, fairness, reviewability and institutional accountability. It concludes that explainable real-time case management should be designed as governed decision infrastructure rather than as an isolated prediction model.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is increasingly important for ensuring transparency and trust in neural systems; however, its applicability to creative text generation remains limited. Neural poetry generation models produce linguistically coherent and stylistically rich outputs, yet explaining decisions such as metaphor construction, emotional tone, and thematic development remains unresolved. This systematic literature review synthesizes 26 peer‐reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2026, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines and a predefined protocol across four major digital libraries. The analysis identifies a fundamental mismatch between existing XAI paradigms and the properties of generative modeling. We propose a taxonomy distinguishing classification‐native methods from generation‐compatible approaches, highlighting their differing assumptions. Based on established criteria of contrastivity, selectivity, and faithfulness, we show that attention mechanisms lack causal validity as explanatory tools. To consolidate these findings, we introduce a unified failure framework comprising five interacting structural limitations: token–semantic mismatch, attention non‐causality, classification–generation incompatibility, evaluation collapse, and human–model ontological misalignment. These limitations collectively constrain the effectiveness of current XAI methods in creative contexts. Our findings indicate that advancing explainability in neural poetry generation requires a shift toward semantic‐level representations, causal intervention‐based approaches, and human‐centered evaluation frameworks that incorporate aesthetic and interpretive dimensions.

Automated decision-making systems increasingly influence healthcare, finance, recruitment, education, public administration, and digital platforms. Although advanced machine-learning models can discover complex relationships, their opaque reasoning can obstruct auditing, contestability, and safe deployment. This narrative review examines how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) may improve transparency and reliability by clarifying model behavior, revealing data dependencies, supporting error detection, and enabling informed human oversight. It synthesizes established work on interpretable modeling, local feature attribution, surrogate explanations, counterfactual reasoning, explanation evaluation, and governance. A conceptual assurance framework connects data provenance, predictive validation, explanation fidelity, subgroup analysis, and operational monitoring. The paper distinguishes understandable explanations from evidence that a system is accurate, robust, or fair: an attractive explanation alone does not establish reliability. A non-empirical diagram illustrates complementary assurance dimensions without implying measured results. Practical implications include tailoring explanations to decision recipients, testing explanation stability under perturbations, documenting uncertainty, and establishing appeal mechanisms. The review concludes that XAI is most effective when embedded within a wider socio-technical accountability process rather than deployed as a stand-alone visualization technique.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Fiber-reinforced polymer (FRP) composites offer high specific strength, high stiffness, and good corrosion resistance, which makes them suitable for aerospace, automotive, marine, and wind-energy structures. Their interlaminar fracture behavior is harder to pin down because delamination testing is slow and costly and the response shifts with loading mode. This study presents an explainable hybrid machine learning framework for interlaminar fracture toughness under Mode-I, Mode-II, and Mixed-Mode loading. A weighted ensemble pairs Categorical Boosting (CatBoost), a gradient-boosting method, with the Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN), a pretrained transformer built for tabular data. A Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) tunes the CatBoost hyperparameters and the ensemble weight against specimen-grouped cross-validation. The work draws on the public D-STANDART experimental dataset and treats DCB, ELS, and MMB as three separate prediction problems for GIC, GIIC, and GC rather than pooling them into one model. The analyzed D-STANDART specimens comprise pultruded carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP) material based on Zoltek PX35 carbon fiber. The data are partitioned at the specimen level, so no specimen contributes records to more than one subset, and feature selection uses the training data alone. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) then measure how each input shifts the predicted toughness in each mode. The framework reached an R2 of 0.9280 for DCB, 0.9870 for ELS, and 0.9627 for MMB, with RMSE values of 5.1759, 1.5041, and 2.8809 and MAE values of 1.6502, 0.5372, and 0.7000, respectively. Bringing a tabular foundation model into delamination analysis, and keeping the three loading modes apart, lets the framework report mode-specific feature behavior instead of one averaged picture.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into education has received increasing attention over the past couple of years. However, the perceived impacts of such technologies by trilingual learners have remained unaddressed by scholars. Compared with conventional second or foreign language learners, trilingual learners may need to coordinate languages with different levels of proficiency and functions while also coping with unequal AI support across languages. To fill the gap, this descriptive qualitative study drew on technology acceptance model (TAM) and control‐value theory (CVT) to examine Mongolian trilingual learners’ perceptions about the academic and affective impacts of AI tools. A sample of 40 Mongolian trilingual students in Inner Mongolia, China were asked to complete an open‐ended questionnaire and attend an interview. The results of thematic analysis demonstrated that AI technologies had imposed several positive and negative academic and affective impacts on trilingual students. Particularly, it was found that AI adoption could improve learning efficiency, autonomy, and agency, but over‐reliance on AI tools might lead to dependency, plagiarism acts, surface learning, and reduced critical thinking. Regarding affective consequences, the students found AI adoption exciting, motivating, and emotionally safe, while they endorsed the possibility of anxiety, stress, fear, emotional tension, and emotional detachment. The study discusses the findings and provides practical implications for trilingual teachers, students, and policymakers by enhancing their AI and emotional literacy.

Conversational recommendation systems help digital platforms elicit user preferences through multi-turn interaction, but they often face a practical tension between recommendation accuracy and interaction cost when users provide vague or low-information inputs. This study follows a design science approach to develop a cost-conscious conversational recommendation artifact for such ambiguous service encounters. The artifact is guided by two design principles. First, retrospective outcome-guided supervision uses successful historical conversion trajectories as downstream anchors for improving responses at earlier low-information states. Second, isolated reflection separates recommendation generation from consistency checking, enabling diagnostic regeneration when candidate responses conflict with previously stated user constraints. In implementation, the artifact instantiates these principles through parameter-efficient adaptation of open-source large language models and prompt-isolated role switching over a shared backbone model. We validate the artifact on three conversational recommendation datasets covering movie and e-commerce settings, using outcome efficacy, interaction efficiency, process analysis, ablation analysis, robustness checks, and human evaluation. Here, interaction efficiency refers to user-visible dialogue turns, while computational burden is reported separately through training, memory, and latency measurements. The empirical results show that the artifact improves recommendation effectiveness while maintaining a favorable balance between interaction burden and conversion outcomes under the tested conditions. Process-level analysis further characterizes how recommendation behavior evolves over the course of dialogue. This study contributes transferable design principles for embedding retrospective preference optimization and isolated reflection into conversational recommendation systems, offering operational guidance for platforms seeking to improve personalization under constraints on interaction cost.

Observatory bibliographies increasingly need to determine not only whether a facility is named in a paper, but how its data support the scientific argument. We frame this need as semantic contribution attribution on a six-level scale (L0-L5), from non-use and mention-only cases to auxiliary, major, and exclusive data support. We present FacilityAudit-Agent, a framework that builds a page-bounded outline of each PDF, enriches sections with roles and facility mentions, and uses a tool-calling large language model (LLM) to fetch text on demand. Evidence from the sections is combined through an explicit decision tree and a coverage-calibrated confidence score, with uncertain cases routed to human review. The framework supports both single-facility and inventory audits and transfers to new facilities without retraining. On a test set of 39,358 human-annotated paper-facility pairs, FacilityAudit-Agent achieves 89.1% accuracy and 79.8% macro-F1 in single_audit mode, outperforming the other three baselines by 5.8, 8.3, and 12.1 accuracy points, respectively, with the clearest gains at L2 and L5. In inventory_audit mode, it also leads in facility listing and in level assignment among listed pairs. Ablations show multi-hop reading and tree indexing matter most for L3-L5. FacilityAudit-Agent has been deployed at the National Astronomical Data Center, where it is responsible for processing publications related to LAMOST, FAST, and EP.

Background Presently, artificial intelligence technology is being extensively applied across clinical nursing practice. However, whether this technology can be deeply integrated into clinical workflows depends largely on nurses’ attitudes and literacy regarding artificial intelligence. Consequently, conducting an in depth exploration of core factors shaping registered nurses’ artificial intelligence attitudes and literacy holds significant importance for driving the rapid development of intelligent nursing. Methods This study strictly adhered to PRISMA guidelines. Systematic searches were conducted across seven English databases, namely PubMed, Web of Science, Medline, Embase, The Cochrane Library, IEEE Xplore, and CINAHL, alongside three Chinese databases, including China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang Data, and VIP Database. The search timeframe ranged from database inception through May 30, 2026. Following screening according to inclusion and exclusion criteria, independent factors influencing attitudes and literacy were extracted. Employing a narrative synthesis approach, these influencing factors were categorized, summarized, and narratively integrated across distinct thematic domains. Results A total of 30 studies involving 12,958 registered nurses were included in this systematic review. The majority of the studies were conducted in China and Turkey. The independent factors influencing registered nurses’ attitudes toward artificial intelligence included educational attainment, age, length of service, gender, professional title/nursing level, hospital tier/category, AI awareness/understanding/knowledge, AI training experience, AI usage experience, artificial intelligence anxiety, and digital leadership. The factors independently affecting nurses’ artificial intelligence literacy included leadership style, AI training experience, and usage experience/frequency. Conclusion Current evidence indicates that key modifiable factors to improve nurses’ attitudes toward and literacy in artificial intelligence include AI-related training, practical hands-on experience, and organizational leadership, while technical anxiety should not be overlooked. Compared with demographic characteristics, educational and experiential interventions appear more effective in enhancing nurses’ artificial intelligence literacy levels. Nursing managers should actively implement smart training programs, increase opportunities for nurses to apply new technologies in clinical practice, and formulate relevant policies regarding data privacy protection and accountability division, thereby promoting the safe and effective integration of AI technology into patient care. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/recorddashboard
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Distilled text-to-image models generate images quickly, but classifiers trained on those images can perform substantially worse than classifiers trained on images from their slower base models. We adapt released distilled generators to produce better training data while retaining fast generation. We fit a low-rank update to the student's first prediction so that it reaches an intermediate state produced by its unguided base, then disable the update and let the unchanged student finish generation. The base supplies training targets and is absent at inference. Guided targets and shorter jumps give classifiers lower accuracy in our ablations, showing why the state used for supervision matters. Across three generator families, the adapted images train better classifiers than images from the released students. With class-name templates at full ImageNet-1k scale, ResNet-50 top-1 rises from 8.4% to 34.2% for FLUX.2-klein and from 12.7% to 32.1% for SD-Turbo, using two and three denoiser evaluations per image, respectively. Fixed adapters also improve results on additional classes, fine-grained datasets, and other learner architectures and training recipes. Template-based adaptation remains useful against richer-prompt alternatives, while the benefit of combining adaptation with LLM generation prompts depends on the generator. Adapting a single generation step makes fast generators substantially more useful for training visual models.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Population aging and rapid digitalization have intensified concerns about older adults’ digital participation. Although access disparities have narrowed, older adults continue to differ from younger groups in how they use digital technologies, with their use skewed toward instrumental rather than hedonic purposes. Technophobia is a salient psychological barrier; yet, its distinct fear dimensions and their links to different forms of technology use remain insufficiently differentiated. Daily technical support (DTS) may provide an important sociotechnical context for understanding these relationships. Objective This study aimed to test how DTS promotes older adults’ instrumental and hedonic technology use by reducing multidimensional technophobia (fear of inconvenience, fear of personal failure, and human-machine ambiguity) and whether these mechanisms differ by gender. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among Chinese adults aged ≥55 years recruited via online platforms and offline communities in Nanjing (June-October 2024). A total of 212 valid responses were included (mean age 66.96, SD 6.96, range 55‐86 years; 142/212, 68.4% women). Measures assessed day-to-day technical support, 3 dimensions of technophobia, instrumental versus hedonic technology use, and demographic variables. We used partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5000 bootstrap resamples to test direct, indirect, and moderated mediation effects, reporting 95% bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) CI. Results DTS significantly reduced fear of inconvenience (β=−0.455, 95% BCa CI −0.632 to −0.229; P <.001) but did not significantly affect fear of personal failure ( P =.12) or human-machine ambiguity ( P =.26). Fear of inconvenience and human-machine ambiguity negatively predicted instrumental use (IU; β=−0.215, 95% BCa CI −0.410 to −0.009; P =.05 and β=−0.211, 95% BCa CI −0.389 to −0.001; P =.04). DTS had a positive direct effect on IU (β=0.104, 95% BCa CI 0.009 to 0.203; P =.04) but not on hedonic use (HU; β=0.075; P =.11). The indirect effect of DTS on IU through fear of inconvenience was significant (β=0.097, 95% BCa CI 0.020-0.204). Gender moderated the effect of DTS on fear of inconvenience (β=0.287, 95% BCa CI 0.052-0.518; P =.02), and such conditional indirect effect was significant for men (β=0.098, 95% BCa CI 0.001-0.219) but not for women (β=0.036, 95% BCa CI −0.002 to 0.116). Conclusions DTS was associated with greater instrumental technology use among older adults through lower fear of inconvenience, with a stronger indirect association among men, whereas no comparable pathway emerged for HU. This suggests that gender may shape how older adults benefit psychologically from technical support rather than reflect general differences in support needs. Interventions should move beyond one-size-fits-all approaches by providing targeted, task-oriented support that addresses older adults’ specific technological fears and practical barriers.

Financial technology (fintech) is changing how financial markets operate and how investors access, interpret, and act on financial information. Digital payments, mobile investment platforms, robo-advisory services, artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, big-data analytics, blockchain, and automated trading have altered the speed, reach, and informational basis of financial decisions. Yet the consequences are not uniformly beneficial: greater access and analytical capacity can coexist with cyber risk, algorithmic opacity, behavioural overconfidence, platform dependence, and unequal digital capabilities. This conceptual study synthesizes the literature review supplied for the paper, which covers fintech adoption, digital transformation in financial services, capital-market infrastructure, AI-supported investment decisions, financial risk management, mutual-fund choice, and the behavioural implications of personal-finance applications. The study proposes an integrated conceptual model linking fintech capabilities to investment decision-making quality through information accessibility, analytical support, transaction efficiency, and trust. Behavioural biases act as mediators, while financial literacy, digital capability, and governance quality moderate the proposed relationships. Expected outcomes include decision quality, portfolio alignment, participation, and market efficiency, subject to risks and institutional conditions. The model is conceptual and is not presented as empirically validated. It offers propositions for future testing and practical implications for investors, fintech providers, financial institutions, and regulators. The central argument is that fintech creates value when technological capability is combined with informed users, transparent design, robust safeguards, and meaningful human oversight.

Cognitive workload estimation from physiological signals is increasingly relevant in high-risk environments, where continuous and unobtrusive monitoring can inform adaptive systems and safety interventions. This paper presents FOCUS (Frequency-band Optimized Cognitive-load Ultralight SSM), a compact Mamba-2-based model for EEG-based binary workload classification under constrained data conditions. Rather than learning frequency sensitivity from data, FOCUS encodes preprocessed multi-channel EEG using a fixed FFT decomposition that covers the five canonical EEG bands. The proposed model combines depthwise-separable convolution and a weight-shared encoder-bottleneck Mamba-2 pair, with 0.04 million parameters and 0.11 GFLOPs. Evaluated in a pilot study with 11 participants under leave-one-subject-out cross-validation across three cognitively distinct tasks, FOCUS achieves 74.75% accuracy on the full dataset at 0.08 ms GPU model-forward latency. In the weight-sharing ablation, the shared configuration achieves 4.55 percentage points higher accuracy on the full dataset than the non-shared variant while reducing the SSM parameter budget; however, this difference does not reach statistical significance under a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test ($p=0.083$). Overall, the selected FOCUS configuration provides a favorable trade-off between classification performance and computational cost within this controlled pilot setting.

Abstract In this work, we introduce Segmentation to Human–Object Interaction (Seg2HOI), a novel framework that integrates segmentation-based vision foundation models with the human–object interaction (HOI) task, distinguished from traditional detection-based HOI methods. Our approach enhances HOI detection by not only predicting the standard triplets but also introducing quadruplets, which extend HOI triplets by including segmentation masks for human–object pairs. More specifically, Seg2HOI inherits the properties of the vision foundation model (e.g., promptable and interactive mechanisms) and incorporates an implicit relation-learning decoder that applies these attributes to the HOI task. By freezing the vision foundation model, Seg2HOI preserves its original capabilities while using pixel-level mask guidance to support high-level relational reasoning. Despite being trained only for the HOI task, without additional training mechanisms for these properties, the framework demonstrates that such features still operate efficiently. Extensive experiments on two public benchmark datasets demonstrate that Seg2HOI achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods, even in zero-shot scenarios. Lastly, we propose that Seg2HOI can generate HOI quadruplets and interactive HOI segmentation from novel text and visual prompts that were not used during training, making it versatile for a wide range of applications by leveraging this flexibility.

Accurate early-stage prediction of cascading failure severity is essential for assessing the vulnerability of power transmission networks. However, existing data-driven approaches often rely on network-specific representations, limiting their generalizability across power system topologies. This work investigates the complementary capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for cascading failure severity prediction. First, standalone LLM predictors are developed using a LoRA-fine-tuned LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct model with varying degrees of topological information. A hybrid Graph-LLM fusion framework is then proposed, integrating a Topology-Aware Graph Attention Transformer (TAGAT) with the LLM through confidence-gated fusion. TAGAT captures structural dependencies among transmission lines, while the LLM extracts representations from early-stage power-flow observations and aggregated cascade descriptors. The frameworks are evaluated on 30,000 simulated cascading failure scenarios for each of the IEEE 118-bus and IEEE 300-bus systems. Using only the first four cascade steps, the hybrid framework achieves weighted F1 scores of 0.94 and 0.92, respectively. In cross-system transfer from IEEE 118-bus to IEEE 300-bus, it achieves 0.72 zero-shot accuracy, improving to 0.83 with limited target-system calibration, outperforming standalone models and conventional baselines. These results show the potential of combining graph-based structural learning with foundation models to improve cascading failure severity prediction and cross-system transferability.

This research presents a comprehensive synthesis of the principal mathematical, computational, and theoretical achievements of the Four Null Causal Spacetime research program. The research begins with a foundational question: Can four future directed lightlike vectors, arranged in regular tetrahedral spatial directions, provide the causal structure from which four dimensional spacetime geometry and its physical interactions can be reconstructed? Starting from this geometric construction, the program investigates connections between Lorentzian spacetime, general relativity, discrete gravity, electromagnetism, gravitational waves, causal propagation, and quantum field theory. The article reviews the development of the research through Parts I–XVII and the integrated research updates of 22 October 2026. Its principal topics and reported achievements include: Foundational geometry: Exact tetrahedral incidence identities, complementary three dimensional gradient and circulation sectors, Hodge duality exchange, and Lorentzian metric reconstruction from four null generators. Discrete gravity: A four-dimensional parallelotope subdivided into 24 four simplices, with 15 edge variables decomposed into ten metric components and five auxiliary directions. Einstein gravity correspondence: Recovery of the Fierz Pauli operator, two physical gravitational wave polarizations, Newtonian gravity, and standard weak-field PPN coefficients within the stated assumptions. Nonlinear gravitational interactions: Exact agreement in 1,440,000 coefficient comparisons for the leading Einstein cubic interaction, together with additional numerical quartic correspondence tests. Gravitational stability: Identification of an unstable microscopic scalar mode with growth magnitude approximately 2.890053638, motivating the development of Formulation A. Characteristic null dynamics: A constrained null ray architecture incorporating radiative shear, scalar and vector constraints, relational time, and a stable free spin 2 sector. Electromagnetism and quantum universality: Independent Maxwell discretizations with matching infrared photon properties, gauge identities, scalar QED infrared behavior, and leading gravity photon coupling. Causal propagation: Computational tests of conserved gravitational curvature disturbances propagating within the relativistic future light cone. Null boundary geometry: Canonical area boost variables, exact cancellation of internal edge contributions under matched null ray gluing, and connections with published null gravity formulations. Quantum gravity connections: Exact four simplex combinatorial correspondences, semiclassical group field theory compatibility, a leading soft-graviton factorization theorem candidate, and a partial covariant effective field theory gauge completion construction. The essay also examines unsuccessful approaches, mathematical limitations, and unresolved physical questions. In particular, a complete stable nonlinear microscopic gravitational evolution law and a fully derived quantum theory of gravity have not yet been established. Pharmaceutical companies maintain vast archives of legacy preclinical study reports that contain study-context details, such as fasting, anesthesia, and laboratory instrumentation, that are rarely captured in structured data formats, yet they can correlate with clinical pathology parameters values and limit the reuse of historical data. This work demonstrates practical, scalable solutions to recover such descriptors from heterogeneous report texts using large language model (LLM)-based extraction pipelines developed independently by two industry teams. The pipelines identify and normalize metadata fields and return verbatim evidence with page and section reference, hasting human verification and iterative refinement. Evaluation of over 400 documents against expert-curated reference values showed high agreement across a broad set of metadata fields. Performance was strongest for consistently reported items and lower for descriptors subject to linguistic or report structure variability. Extraction time has shrunk from 25 minutes in the manual benchmark to 1.6 minutes. As a concrete biological demonstration, we show that fasting status extracted from report text was associated with species- and analyte-specific shifts in clinical chemistry parameters, illustrating how recovered metadata can improve selection of historical controls. Key strengths of the approach are scalability, traceability, and the ability to recover information missing from current industry standards. Main limitations are dependence on source-report quality and initial expert effort to define and refine schemas. These results establish how LLMs can convert heterogeneous, unstructured legacy reports into evidence-grounded, reusable and structured metadata, leading to better experimental comparability, and thus enabling reliable data pooling or informed virtual control selection.

ABSTRACT This critical review traces the evolution of machine learning (ML) across the full value chain of heterogeneous catalysis over 2017–2026, from catalyst discovery to reactor and process design, and across the principal reaction families (CO 2 reduction, water splitting, nitrogen chemistry, zeolite‐catalyzed transformations). Each stage is evaluated against four criteria — data foundation, method maturity, experimental validation and deployment readiness — through a structured capability scorecard. Digitalization has advanced from the top of the length scale downward: prediction of adsorption energies and atomistic potential‐energy surfaces is now mature, with errors of tens of meV relative to the reference DFT calculations and accelerations of three orders of magnitude over DFT, yet experimentally validated catalyst improvements remain rare. The most significant advance is the closed‐loop autonomous laboratory coupling Bayesian optimization, automated synthesis and high‐throughput testing. Large language models have begun to add a reasoning and orchestration layer, while kinetics, reactor and process design remain the least digitalized stages. We argue that the field's next decade of impact will be decided not by more accurate atomic‐scale prediction but by carrying ML into experimental validation and the reactor‐and‐process scale, where catalysis is hardest to industrialize and where data‐driven methods are weakest.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the content of accounting work, but the career consequences of that change remain less clear in emerging economies. Using field responses from 600 accounting and finance professionals in Nigeria, Ghana, and Kenya (200 per country), this paper examines whether intensive AI use is associated with professional role transformation, whether role transformation is associated with competence evolution, and whether those evolving competencies are linked to career sustainability. Learning and organizational support is considered both as a contextual resource and as a potential moderator. The analysis uses multi-item composite measures, HC3-robust path regressions, 5,000-resample bootstrapping, effect-size estimates, 10-fold cross-validation, and exploratory country comparisons. AI adoption was positively associated with role transformation (β = .491, p < .001). AI adoption (β = .286, p < .001) and role transformation (β = .462, p < .001) jointly explained 42.6% of the variance in competence evolution, while competence evolution was positively associated with career sustainability (β = .414, p < .001). The direct role-transformation effect on career sustainability was negligible (β = .013, p = .764), whereas the indirect effect through competence evolution was significant (β = .192, 95% bootstrap CI [.146, .242]). The serial pathway from AI adoption through role transformation and competence evolution to career sustainability was also significant (β = .094, 95% CI [.069, .123]). Learning and organizational support had a positive main effect but did not moderate the competence-sustainability relationship. The results suggest that the long-term value of AI-related role change depends less on the fact that work changes than on whether professionals acquire the digital, analytical, advisory, and ethical capabilities needed to succeed in the redesigned role. Keywords: artificial intelligence; accounting profession; role transformation; competence evolution; career sustainability; emerging economies; Africa; human capital.

documents.abstract: This study examines the associations among occupational health and safety awareness, OHS performance, employee voice, and organizational trust from a social work perspective. Although previous studies have examined occupational health and safety, employee voice, and organizational trust separately, limited attention has been paid to how these variables operate together within a rights-based and empowerment-oriented social work framework. Data collected from 400 factory employees were analyzed using correlation analysis, multiple regression analysis, and PROCESS Model 6. The findings showed that greater awareness was significantly associated with organizational trust through both direct and indirect pathways. OHS performance and employee voice were significant mediators, and the sequential indirect effect through OHS performance and employee voice was statistically significant. Rather than introducing previously unexamined associations, the study integrates established workplace variables within a sequential model and interprets their combined relevance for rights-based education, employee participation, and workplace social work practice.
